sections.h2: Office location and what it does
sections.html:
You will find the Register of Deeds in the City-County Building, 400 Main Street, Suite 225, Knoxville, TN 37902. The main number is 865-215-2330, and records staff answer at 865-215-2329. Weekday counter hours are eight to half past four. The office website describes it as a recording agency only. It files deeds, deeds of trust, liens, lien releases, powers of attorney, bonds and plats. Staff cannot write your deed or give legal advice, so plan to use your closing attorney or title company for anything beyond filing. Call 865-215-2329 with questions about the process itself.

Only land inside Knox County can be recorded here, and a deed for a house in a neighboring county will be sent back. Handwritten records reach back to the late 1700s. Every record is public except military discharges.

To search, start with an owner's name, a legal description and a rough recording date. Clear title still needs a title company or abstractor to confirm it, because liens, easements and court judgments are not all filed in this office.

Tennessee statute sets the recording fees, which appear on the county's fee schedule. For a warranty, quitclaim or trust deed, the first two pages cost $12.00 and each extra page costs $5.00. Add $1.00 for taxable documents. Certified copies are $1.00 a page. An online fee calculator lets you estimate the total before filing.

Common Knox County recording charges

Transfer tax is charged on the value of the sale. Mortgage tax applies to a deed of trust once the exempt first portion is set aside. The closing agent will give you the exact totals for your transaction.

sections.h2: What a deed needs to be accepted
sections.html:
A filing requirements page spells out what warranty, quitclaim and trustee's deeds need. Most delays come from a missing item, so walk through these points before the deed leaves the closing table:

  • The land lies in Knox County, and the preparer's name and complete address are on the deed
  • Seller signatures are notarized, and an original is presented
  • The buyer's name and address appear, along with the responsible taxpayer
  • Value and consideration are stated, and the value is taxable
  • The prior deed is cited by instrument number or by book and page, and a legal description is included

A warranty deed can show $0.00 consideration only between spouses, for an exempt entity, or when property moves into a revocable living trust. A trustee's deed or substitute trustee's deed must carry a trust deed reference and an appointment reference. Other reasons for rejection include names too faint to index, a copied notary seal, a missing exhibit, or a missing chain of title.

Bring photo identification to the signing and sign in front of the notary, not before. Notarization is the preferred method, though two witnesses can also work. Plats are accepted in two sizes only: 24 by 36 inches and 18 by 24 inches.

Most filings are recorded the same day they arrive. Staff checks that the document is recordable and the fees are right, assigns an instrument number, scans it, indexes it and verifies the data, which usually takes a day. The original then goes back to the filer. Tennessee sets no time limit for recording a deed, but the office recommends doing it quickly, since an unrecorded deed invites legal trouble.

The website offers e-recording, a request form for deed copies and a lien release form. After a mortgage is paid off, the lender files a release with the register, and you can get a copy from the office. If you lose your deed, the recording is the primary evidence of ownership, and a certified copy works as the original.

A change in ownership generally requires a new deed recorded here. The exceptions are court cases such as probate, divorce or foreclosure, and certain deaths where the right language exists and a death certificate is recorded. Adding or removing a name also takes a newly prepared deed, and the office suggests an attorney or title company prepare it.

Property fraud is a real risk in county records, so the office runs a free Fraud Notification System at alertme.knoxrod.org. Owners enter their names and get an email whenever a document under a matching name is recorded.

The office also publishes reports that help a seller price and time a sale:

  • A weekly real estate transfers report, sortable by value, with an email signup
  • Reports on money borrowed against real estate and taxes collected on mortgage records and transfers
  • A top lenders report showing every lender, the amount loaned and the number of loans in Knox County
  • Historic tax maps from the 1950s and 1980s, plus a legacy deed search

Military discharge papers (DD214s) can be recorded here at no fee, and those records stay confidential.

sections.h2: Where this office fits in a sale
sections.html:
In Knox County, a sale finishes at this office. Deed, transfer tax and recording fee all go here, and the staff recommends having an attorney or title company prepare the deed. Ask your closing agent who will file it and when. After recording, the Property Assessor changes the owner's name, which can take as long as a week.

For a seller the sequence looks like this: the title company prepares the deed, you sign before a notary, the closing agent submits it with the fees, and the office assigns an instrument number once it is indexed. Keep the certified copy for your records, since it works as the original. If you are selling an inherited house, check that the deed that put the estate's name or your name on the property is itself recorded, because the new deed refers back to it by instrument number or book and page. A missing link in that chain is a common reason a deed comes back unrecorded.

Before closing, ask the Trustee about any unpaid county tax so it can be cleared at the table. Locally, the county had 232,546 housing units and 5,013 building permits in 2025, so this office handles a steady stream of deeds and mortgage releases. For a house with a cloudy history, such as an inherited property, a title company can trace the recorded chain and tell you what needs fixing before the deed is signed.

faqs.q: What do Knox County deed filings cost?
faqs.a: The base charge is $12.00 for a deed of up to two pages, then $5.00 for every extra page, plus $1.00 on taxable documents. The property transfer tax is $0.37 for each $100 of value.

faqs.q: Does a Knox County deed have to be notarized?
faqs.a: Yes. Seller signatures must be notarized, or witnessed by two people, and the original has to be presented. A notary is the preferred method.

faqs.q: Does Tennessee set a deadline for recording a deed in Knox County?
faqs.a: No. Tennessee sets no time limit, but the Register of Deeds recommends recording as soon as possible after the sale to avoid legal problems.

faqs.q: Can a deed carry no sale price?
faqs.a: Only in limited cases. A warranty deed can show $0.00 consideration between spouses, for an exempt entity, or when property is moved into a revocable living trust.

faqs.q: Where can I get a copy of a deed recorded in Knox County?
faqs.a: Request one through the Register of Deeds website or call 865-215-2329. A certified copy is $1.00 per page and acts as the original document.
